prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Bless Tuesday, blessed Monday. Bless the word week, its seven small days trail with y. Bless the men whose words I was too young to hear. A whisper loves a canal. Bless my laugh, lent by grief, I have so little left to borrow. But my hair, it grows— if hair be gold, cut mine so I might rid my beloved of his student loans. Bless thieves, universities, those hands caress what’s not theirs. Bless thinking it was yours. Here are hands, blessed one. Bless them holding the door. Bless each crier on the F train before and after me as they blush, as they transfer into tunnels for the red line. Oh bless, bless wildly, what remains to be done. Bless the one who told me so, the ones who didn’t. Even weak breaths bless. Bless weakness, fragile fortress, my friend’s body absent of soundness. Bless the sound of someone reliable answering your call, saying If you’re going through hell, Hello.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem explores grief, precarity, love, illness, debt, and urban loneliness through a litany of blessings that transforms ordinary people, objects, and moments into sites of tenderness. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Bless, Tuesday, Monday

outputs.L1: Blessed Tuesday, blessed Monday. Blessed be the workweek, its seven small days trailing with y. Blessed be the men whose words I was too young to hear. A whisper loves a canal. Bless my laugh, lent by grief; I have so little left to borrow. But my hair—it grows. If hair be gold, cut mine, so I might rid my beloved of his student loans. Bless thieves, universities, those hands that caress what is not theirs. Bless the belief that it was yours. Here are hands, blessed one. Bless them holding the door. Bless each crier on the F train, before and after me, as they blush, as they transfer into tunnels for the red line. Oh, bless—bless wildly—what remains to be done. Bless the one who told me so, and the ones who did not. Even weak breaths bless. Bless weakness, fragile fortress, my friend’s body absent of soundness. Bless the sound of someone reliable answering your call, saying: If you’re going through hell, hello.
outputs.L2: Praise Tuesday; praise Monday too. Praise the word “week,” its chain of seven little days dragging a “y” behind them. Praise the men whose speech I was not old enough to understand. A murmur is fond of a canal. Praise my laughter, loaned to me by sorrow; I have almost nothing else left to take on credit. Yet my hair keeps growing—if hair counts as gold, shear mine off so I can free my beloved from his student debt. Praise robbers, praise universities, praise the hands that stroke what belongs to someone else. Praise the mistake of believing it was yours. Here are my hands, holy one. Praise them as they keep the door open. Praise every person who weeps on the F train before me and after me, reddening, switching through underground passages toward the red line. Oh, praise—praise recklessly—the work still unfinished. Praise the person who said it to me, and the people who never did. Even faint breathing offers blessing. Praise frailty, that delicate stronghold, my friend’s body lacking health. Praise the sound of a dependable person picking up your call and saying, “If you’re going through hell—hello.”
outputs.L3:
The poem is shaped by a repeated impulse to bless the ordinary. Rather than reserving reverence for grand events or sacred places, the speaker turns toward the basic materials of daily life: time passing, language itself, familiar routines, and the small structures that help people continue. This act of blessing gives dignity to things that might otherwise seem plain or overlooked. Ordinary time becomes meaningful; everyday words become worthy of care; the minor frameworks that hold life together become sources of quiet grace.

At the same time, the poem presents human experience as deeply mixed. Grief, laughter, weakness, and survival are not treated as separate or opposing states, but as intertwined realities. The speaker recognizes that people often laugh while suffering, endure while feeling fragile, and carry sorrow even as they go on living. This mixture gives the poem much of its emotional power. It does not simplify pain or pretend that survival is easy, but it acknowledges the strange, resilient ways people continue through hardship.

The speaker also reflects on debt, ownership, theft, and institutions with a tone that blends irony and tenderness. These subjects might suggest systems of power, obligation, and control, yet the poem approaches them in a human and often wry manner. The speaker seems aware of the absurdities and injustices built into social and economic life, but also attentive to the vulnerable people caught within those systems. This creates a balance between critique and compassion: the poem can question institutions while still caring for the individuals who live under their pressures.

A central part of the poem’s generosity lies in its attention to strangers and fellow sufferers in public spaces. The speaker honors people moving through the world with private burdens, especially those crying on the train. Such figures are usually passed by, ignored, or politely unseen, but the poem pauses to recognize them. In doing so, it transforms a public scene into a moment of shared humanity. The crying stranger becomes not an interruption but a presence deserving tenderness, respect, and blessing.

By the end, the poem turns toward the consolations of reliability, friendship, and response. After moving through grief, irony, public sorrow, and the fragile routines of life, it closes by blessing the comfort of someone who answers in a moment of hardship. This ending suggests that survival often depends on simple forms of dependability: a person who picks up the phone, a friend who remains present, a voice that meets distress with care. The poem ultimately affirms that amid uncertainty and suffering, connection itself can become a kind of blessing.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a world marked by grief, precarity, illness, debt, and urban loneliness, yet it does so through the repeated gesture of blessing. Its litany gathers ordinary people, objects, and moments—those who are sick, tired, poor, afraid, in love, or simply trying to survive—and turns them into sites of tenderness and attention. Rather than reserving holiness for what is pure, successful, or untouched by suffering, the poem extends blessing to the fragile and damaged parts of life: the unpaid bill, the hospital room, the exhausted body, the lonely apartment, the brief encounter, the small act of care.

Through this structure, the poem suggests that blessing is not a denial of pain but a way of staying with it. The repetition creates a rhythm of compassion, as if each blessing makes room for another form of human vulnerability. The poem recognizes that people often live under heavy pressures—economic hardship, emotional loss, bodily weakness, isolation—yet it refuses to let these conditions define them only as victims. Instead, it finds dignity in endurance and beauty in what remains.

Love, in the poem, appears not as something grand or untouched by difficulty, but as something that persists within difficulty. It is found in care, memory, survival, and the willingness to see one another clearly. Even weakness becomes a kind of connection, because it reveals how dependent people are on one another. Loss and suffering, while never romanticized, become places where tenderness can still appear.

Ultimately, the poem argues that to bless is to pay attention with compassion. By blessing the wounded, the ordinary, and the overlooked, the poem transforms a harsh urban landscape into a space where connection is still possible. It suggests that endurance does not come from escaping pain completely, but from recognizing and honoring what remains after pain has done its work. In this sense, blessing becomes a form of resistance, a way of being held, and a way of continuing to live.
outputs.L5: Monday is often seen as the start of a new journey, a fresh chance to set goals and move forward with hope. As Monday passes and Tuesday arrives, we can choose to bless the day with a positive heart, kind words, and a grateful spirit. May this Tuesday bring peace, strength, and new opportunities. Let every step be guided by patience, every challenge met with courage, and every moment filled with purpose. Bless this Tuesday and make it a day of progress, joy, and inspiration.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary prose poem in the form of a blessing/litany, full of grief, wordplay, tenderness, and surreal urban details like the F train, student loans, and unreliable bodies.
counterfactuals.output:
Blessed be the F train arriving late and lit from within like an apology. Blessed be the platform saxophonist playing “Autumn Leaves” in July, his case open like a small, velvet hunger. Blessed be the rats who know the city better than we do, who inherit our crumbs and curses, who keep moving.

Blessed be the student loans accruing interest in the dark, little ghosts with calculators, little gods of compounding grief. Blessed be the hold music, the password reset, the email that begins We regret to inform you and means it. Blessed be the degree framed crooked on the wall, paper boat on a flood.

Blessed be our unreliable bodies: the knee that predicts rain, the gut that revolts, the brain fog rolling in like a rent increase. Blessed be the heart, that unpaid intern, showing up every day with coffee and bad boundaries. Blessed be the cells misreading the memo. Blessed be the blood, the ache, the flare, the tremor, the dizzy spell in the cereal aisle. Blessed be the friend who sits down on the linoleum beside us and does not ask us to be brave.

Blessed be the bodega cat sleeping on the ATM, guardian of cash we do not have. Blessed be the bruised banana, the two-dollar coffee, the umbrella turned inside out like a black flower in traffic. Blessed be the siren’s red grammar, the laundromat’s lunar windows, the pigeons wearing their oil-slick suits to every funeral.

Blessed be the dead, who keep texting from inside ordinary objects: a chipped mug, a wool scarf, a song leaking from a passing car. Blessed be the name we cannot say without becoming weather. Blessed be the empty chair, that faithful animal. Blessed be the photograph where everyone is younger and no one knows it.

Blessed be the living, too, though we are so hard to keep. We spill. We cancel. We forget the soup on the stove. We love with cracked screens and low battery. We make a home from extension cords, thrifted lamps, and the miracle of someone saying I’m almost there when the train is stalled under the river.

Blessed be almost. Blessed be not yet. Blessed be the tiny green shoot shouldering through concrete outside the check-cashing place. Blessed be the moon reflected in a pothole and therefore doubled. Blessed be the hands that hold the railing, the hands that hold the phone, the hands that hold another hand because the news is unbearable again.

And blessed be you, beloved disaster, soft machine, city of one. May your debts lose your address. May your pain misplace its keys. May the F train come when you need it, and if it does not, may someone be waiting with a coat, a joke, a paper cup of something hot. May you be forgiven for every day you could only survive. May you survive, and survive, and one morning find yourself laughing—your mouth full of light, your pockets full of impossible flowers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem that begins with “Bless Tuesday, blessed Monday” and keeps repeating “Bless,” moving associatively through loss, hair, universities, thieves, subway crying, illness, and a friend answering the phone.
counterfactuals.output:
Bless Tuesday, blessed Monday,  
Bless the calendar with its torn-out teeth,  
Bless the cup left cold beside the bed,  
Bless the name I almost said and swallowed.  

Bless loss, that room with all the windows open,  
Bless the coat still holding the shape of a shoulder,  
Bless the photograph silvering at the edges,  
Bless the keys that fit a door no longer ours.  

Bless hair in the brush, hair in the drain,  
Bless the black braid cut for mourning,  
Bless the first gray strand shining like a wire,  
Bless the barber’s floor, its soft little ruins.  

Bless the universities with their bells and brick,  
Bless lecture halls where rain taps the glass,  
Bless the student sleeping over a book,  
Bless the thesis unfinished, the bright debt of it.  

Bless thieves, their quick hands, their hunger,  
Bless the wallet gone like a small moon,  
Bless what was taken and what could not be,  
Bless the alley, bless the siren, bless the dark.  

Bless the subway and its underground weather,  
Bless the woman crying into her scarf,  
Bless everyone pretending not to see,  
Bless the train arriving with its terrible light.  

Bless illness, the white room, the beeping star,  
Bless the pill cup, the chart, the needle’s kiss,  
Bless the body trying to remain a body,  
Bless the fever speaking in a childhood tongue.  

Bless the phone ringing after midnight,  
Bless the friend who answers, breathless, awake,  
Bless the little yes that crosses the wire,  
Bless the voice saying, I’m here, I’m here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental lyric paragraph in a modern poetry style: fragmented but emotionally coherent, blessing ordinary and painful things, with themes of debt, grief, public transit, friendship, and survival.
counterfactuals.output: Bless the overdraft blinking like a small red saint on my phone, bless the bus kneeling at the curb to take us in, wet coats, cracked headphones, everyone carrying a weather only partly visible. Bless my friend who texts “you alive?” and means every syllable, bless the debt collector’s voice for reminding me I still have a name, even mispronounced, even owed. I have been grieving in installments: one coin for the father, one coin for the vanished room, one coin for the self I left standing under fluorescent station light. The train arrives full of strangers and their plastic bags, their lunches, their impossible mornings; we sway together, unpaid choir, bruised fruit in the same paper sack. Bless the late rent, the cold coffee, the shoes with rain coming through, bless the hand that finds another hand in the crowd and does not make a speech about it. We are not healed. We are transferring. We are tapping our cards against the gate until mercy lets us through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poetic monologue that sounds like a prayer written by someone grieving but still funny and strange. Include lines about hair as gold, paying off a beloved’s student loans, crying on the F train, and “If you’re going through hell, Hello.”
counterfactuals.output:
Dear whoever is in charge of the dimmer switch,

Please do not make the morning too bright.  
I am not ready to be discovered by the sun  
in this condition—  
socks mismatched, heart eating crackers in bed,  
face swollen like a saint badly painted.

I have been grieving, yes,  
but also I have been making jokes  
because otherwise my mouth would become a basement  
and who can live down there forever?

Bless the beloved, wherever they are,  
with their hair as gold,  
not metaphorical gold either—  
I mean actual treasure, pirate nonsense,  
a whole economy falling from their head,  
enough to ransom spring from winter.

Lord, I would have paid off their student loans  
if love were a bank account  
and not this weird little raccoon  
washing its hands in the dark.

I would have signed every form,  
clicked every box,  
waited on hold through seventeen versions of “Für Elise,”  
just to hear them say,  
What are you doing, you idiot,  
and laugh like a door opening.

Today I cried on the F train.  
Not beautifully.  
Not like a woman in a French film  
with one tear and excellent posture.  
I cried like a vending machine being shaken for mercy.  
A child stared at me  
with the ancient pity of children,  
and I wanted to tell him:  
Buddy, this is what happens  
when you let another person become a country  
and then they take the maps.

Still, I am here.  
Still, the train kept going.  
Still, some man was eating sunflower seeds  
with the focus of a monk.  
Still, someone’s phone played a song  
that sounded like angels falling down stairs.

If you’re going through hell, Hello.

I stitched that to the inside of my coat  
with thread made of bad advice.  
I wear it proudly.  
I wave at the devils.  
I ask if they validate parking.

Please bless my terrible little survival.  
Bless the microwave dinner.  
Bless the unread books.  
Bless the plant I keep apologizing to.  
Bless the ghosts who refuse to pay rent  
but sometimes wash one dish.

And bless the beloved—  
their golden head, their impossible debt,  
their name still glowing in my throat  
like a coin I swallowed as a child.

Let me miss them without becoming a museum.  
Let me love them without turning into salt.  
Let me laugh at the funeral of what I thought would last,  
not because it isn’t holy,  
but because it is,  
and holiness has always had a strange face.

Amen, or whatever word  
means I am not done yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal “blessing” poem with repetitions of the word bless, mixing sacred language with mundane contemporary life—weekdays, hands, universities, subway transfers, illness, phone calls, and weak breaths.
counterfactuals.output:
Bless the Monday with its cracked blue cup,  
bless the Tuesday blinking in the microwave,  
bless the Wednesday hands washing themselves  
as if absolution were sold in soap.

Bless the hands, bless the hands, bless the hands—  
typing, trembling, holding the receipt,  
holding the railing between stations,  
holding the small heat of a fevered forehead.

Bless the university in its sleep of fluorescent halls,  
bless the lecture on dust, the quiz on sorrow,  
bless the student eating noodles from a paper bowl  
beneath the portrait of a saint nobody remembers.

Bless the subway transfer, O bright descent,  
bless the L to the Q, the Q to the nameless dark,  
bless the pigeons adjudicating crumbs  
like gray-robed judges at the gate of heaven.

Bless the missed call, bless the voicemail,  
bless the mother’s voice made thin by distance,  
bless the phone warm as a minor relic  
against the ear, saying call me, call me.

Bless the illness in its rented room,  
bless the pill split cleanly on the plate,  
bless the thermometer’s little prophecy,  
bless the weak breaths counting themselves backward.

Bless the Friday with its pockets full of lint,  
bless the Saturday haloed by laundromat steam,  
bless the Sunday standing barefoot in the kitchen,  
spooning light from the sink.

Bless what forgets to be holy.  
Bless what cannot rise.  
Bless the elevator sighing between floors.  
Bless the hand that presses the button again.

Bless bless bless the ordinary altar—  
the metro card, the syllabus, the ringing phone,  
the wet umbrella opening like a blackened wing,  
the lungs saying yes, then no, then yes.

Bless us in our coats and notifications.  
Bless us in our calendars and coughing.  
Bless us when we transfer incorrectly  
and arrive, amazed, somewhere else.

Bless the breath, weak as a match in rain.  
Bless the rain.  
Bless the match.  
Bless the dark that bends close to listen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
